etymology: Hebrew shoshannīm, “lilies,” plural of shūshan; the name of a tune, “set to Lilies,” over two psalms, the one a royal wedding-song, the other a cry from deep waters.
biblical_def: Shoshannim, “lilies,” names the air or tune set over the forty-fifth psalm and the sixty-ninth. The forty-fifth is “A Song of loves,” the royal wedding-song of the King and His bride: “My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king” (Psa 45:1). It is no mere epithalamium for Solomon, for the Holy Ghost applies its words directly to the Son: “But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Heb 1:8). Here then the lily-song celebrates Christ the King and the Church His bride, arrayed in glory at His right hand. The sixty-ninth, also “upon Shoshannim,” is a very different lily — the suffering Messiah sunk in mire: “they gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psa 69:21), fulfilled at the cross. So the lily of the King’s wedding and the lily of His passion are bound by one tune. The lily is the flower of the valleys, fair and lowly; Christ Himself is the Lily, beautiful in His humiliation and crowned in His exaltation. Let the bride love the Bridegroom who stooped to the mire that He might raise her to the marriage-feast.
webster_summary: “Lilies”; the tune over the royal wedding-psalm of Christ and His bride, and over a psalm of His passion.

Thus the lily of the wedding and the lily of the passion are joined by one tune.

corruption_summary: A messianic wedding-tune; the entry faces no postmodern redefinition, but the critical refusal to read Psalm 45 of Christ and His Church would reduce the lily-song to a court flattery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to name is the habit of reading the forty-fifth psalm as nothing but a wedding ode for an earthly king, the divine address “Thy throne, O God” softened into mere courtly hyperbole. By that reckoning the lily-song is flattery, not prophecy, and Christ is shut out of His own marriage-psalm.

The principle to recover is that the Holy Ghost is His own interpreter. The Epistle to the Hebrews takes “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” and lays it upon the Son, settling the matter beyond dispute. Shoshannim is therefore a song of Christ the King and the Church His bride; and the same tune over the sixty-ninth psalm binds the wedding to the passion, that the bride may know what her glory cost the Bridegroom.

etymology: Hebrew ‘alāmōth, “maidens, virgins,” from ‘almah, a young woman; understood of the treble or soprano voices, the higher register, set over against Sheminith, the bass.
biblical_def: Alamoth, “maidens,” stands over the forty-sixth psalm, “A Song upon Alamoth” (Psa 46, title), and is named in the order of David’s singers, where certain Levites were appointed “with psalteries on Alamoth” (1Ch 15:20). It is most received as the soprano or treble part — the clear high voices of maidens, or instruments pitched to that register — answering the deep notes of Sheminith, “the eighth.” The forty-sixth is among the grandest of all psalms of confidence: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1), the very psalm from which the Reformer drew his mighty hymn of the fortress-God. That so settled a song of strength should be set to the high and clear voices teaches a sweet lesson: the confidence of the saints is not a grim and grinding thing but a bright and singing one. The maidens lift the treble, the men sustain the bass, and the whole congregation, high and low, proclaims together that God is in the midst of her, she shall not be moved. The church’s praise is full only when every voice the LORD has given finds its appointed place in the song.
webster_summary: “Maidens”; the treble or soprano register of the temple song, answering the bass of Sheminith.

corruption_paragraphs: Alamoth faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it pictures stands against a sour and joyless conception of faith, as though trust in God were a clenched endurance with no song in it. The forty-sixth psalm, set to the bright treble of the maidens, says otherwise: the confidence of the saints is a singing confidence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordered fulness of congregational praise. As the maidens’ treble upon Alamoth answered the men’s bass upon Sheminith, so in the church every voice the LORD has given — high and low, strong and frail — finds its appointed part. None sings alone, and none is silent; the whole assembly proclaims together that God is in the midst of her.

etymology: Hebrew higgāyōn, from hāgāh, “to murmur, to muse, to meditate”; a meditative or resounding strain, the soft murmuring of the harp or the musing of the heart.
biblical_def: Higgaion is a word of two faces, both grown from the same root, which signifies the low murmur of meditation. In the ninth psalm it stands as a musical direction joined to Selah: “the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands. Higgaion. Selah” (Psa 9:16) — a solemn instrumental interlude, the harp musing while the soul ponders the judgment of God. In the ninety-second it names the manner of the playing, “upon the harp with a solemn sound” (Psa 92:3), where “solemn sound” is this same Higgaion, the grave and thoughtful strain. And in the nineteenth it is the meditation of the heart itself: “Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight” (Psa 19:14). So Higgaion binds the music of the harp to the musing of the soul, the outward strain to the inward thought. It teaches that true worship is meditative — not a rush of noise, but a pondered praise, where the instrument and the heart alike murmur upon the works and ways of God. The saint is to play and to think, to sound and to consider, that his praise may be no empty clamor but the acceptable musing of a heart fixed upon the LORD.
webster_summary: A meditative or resounding strain; the soft murmuring of the harp joined to the musing of the heart.

corruption_paragraphs: Higgaion faces no postmodern redefinition, but the meditative worship it commends is much neglected. The age prefers its religion loud and immediate — the surge of volume, the instant feeling — and has little patience for the solemn interlude, the pondered pause, the harp musing low while the soul considers the works of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the place of meditation in praise. Higgaion binds the strain of the harp to the musing of the heart; it teaches that worship is to be thought as well as felt, considered as well as sounded. The blessed man meditates in the law day and night; his praise is no empty clamor but the acceptable musing of a heart fixed upon the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew al-tashchēth, “destroy not,” from al, not, and shāchath, to destroy or corrupt; the name of a tune, likely from a vintage-song, over four psalms of imperilled deliverance.
biblical_def: Al-taschith, “Destroy not,” is the tune set over four psalms — the fifty-seventh, fifty-eighth, fifty-ninth, and seventy-fifth. Three are David’s, sung in seasons of mortal peril; the fifty-seventh bears the title, “Altaschith, Michtam of David, when he fled from Saul in the cave” (Psa 57, title). The name appears to be borrowed from an old song of the vintage, for the LORD Himself uses the words of the cluster spared at harvest: “As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one saith, Destroy it not; for a blessing is in it” (Isa 65:8). So the tune carries a gospel in its very name. David, hunted in the cave, pleads in effect what the vinedresser pleads over the bruised cluster: there is a blessing yet within, destroy it not. And the words breathe also of David’s own mercy, who in that same cave forbade the destroying of the LORD’s anointed. Above all, “Destroy not” is the cry of grace over a guilty world: for the sake of the true Cluster, the blessed Seed, the LORD spares a remnant and will not destroy them all. Let the trembling saint take up the tune; the God who spares the cluster for the wine’s sake will not cast away the soul that hides in Him.
webster_summary: “Destroy not”; a tune, likely from a vintage-song, over four psalms of imperilled deliverance and sparing mercy.

corruption_paragraphs: Al-taschith faces no postmodern redefinition. The temptation it answers is the despair of the hunted soul, which reckons itself already destroyed and ceases to plead. David in the cave teaches a better way: to take up the tune of “Destroy not” and shelter in the shadow of God’s wings until the calamities be overpast.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sparing mercy of God for His own. As the vinedresser spares the bruised cluster because a blessing is in it, so the LORD spares His servants for the sake of the true Cluster, Christ, in whom the blessing dwells. The trembling believer may sing “Destroy not” with confidence; the God who keeps the cluster for the wine’s sake will not cast away the soul that hides in Him.

etymology: Hebrew shūshan ‘ēdūth, “the lily of testimony” (shūshan, a lily; ‘ēdūth, testimony, witness); the tune set over the sixtieth psalm.
biblical_def: Shushan-eduth, “the lily of testimony,” is the tune over the sixtieth psalm: “To the chief Musician upon Shushaneduth, Michtam of David, to teach” (Psa 60, title). The title joins two sweet things — the lily, fair and lowly, the flower of the field, and the testimony, the sure witness of God’s covenant word. The psalm itself was sung in a dark hour, when David strove with the Syrians and Edom, when the people had seen hard things and been made to drink the wine of astonishment. Yet in the midst of it the testimony shines like a lily: “Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth” (Psa 60:4). The lily of testimony is the truth of God lifted up like a standard over a shaken people, beautiful and unbreaking when all else fails. So the believer, in his own day of striving and astonishment, fixes his eye upon the lily that does not wither — the covenant testimony of a God who cannot lie. The banner of His truth is displayed above the battle; they that fear Him rally to it, and are not ashamed.

They that fear Him rally to that standard and are not ashamed; through God they shall do valiantly, for the witness above the battle cannot lie.

etymology: Hebrew shoshannīm ‘ēdūth, “lilies, a testimony” (plural of shūshan, lily, with ‘ēdūth, testimony); the tune set over the eightieth psalm.
biblical_def: Shoshannim-eduth, “lilies, a testimony,” is the plural sister of Shushan-eduth, the tune over the eightieth psalm: “To the chief Musician upon ShoshannimEduth, A Psalm of Asaph” (Psa 80, title). Where the sixtieth lifted a single lily of witness, the eightieth lifts lilies — a whole field of testimony — over the vine of Israel, broken down and burned. It is one of the great psalms of national lament and pleading: “Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock; thou that dwellest between the cherubims, shine forth” (Psa 80:1). Three times its refrain rises like a lily reaching for the sun: “Turn us again, O God, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved” (Psa 80:3). The testimony amid the lilies is that the covenant Shepherd has not forgotten His flock, though the vine be wasted; His face, once shining upon them, is the whole of their salvation. Let the church in her own seasons of ruin take up this tune. The vine that God planted He will yet restore; the lilies of His testimony bloom even over the trampled vineyard, and the prayer “turn us again” is never refused to a people who seek His shining face.
webster_summary: “Lilies, a testimony”; the tune over the eightieth psalm, the lament and pleading over the wasted vine of Israel.

Three times the psalm prays, “Turn us again, cause thy face to shine, and we shall be saved” — confessing that revival is His gift and His shining is the whole of their hope. The vine that God planted He will yet restore to a people who seek His face.

etymology: Hebrew yōnath ‘ēlem rechōqīm, “the silent dove of them that are afar off” (yōnah, a dove; ‘ēlem, silence; rechōqīm, far-off ones); the tune over the fifty-sixth psalm.
biblical_def: Jonath-elem-rechokim, “the silent dove of them that are afar off,” is the tune set over the fifty-sixth psalm, written “when the Philistines took him in Gath” (Psa 56, title). The figure is exquisite and exact. David, driven from the land of Israel and held among the Philistines, was as a dove far from her cote — gentle, defenceless, voiceless among strangers, harmless among hawks. The dove cannot fight; she can only flee and mourn and trust. So the psalm is all trust where there is no strength: “What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee” (Psa 56:3). The exile dove pours out a tender confidence that God marks her every flutter: “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psa 56:8). Here is comfort for every saint who feels himself a stranger far from home, silent and harmless in a hostile place. The God who watches the dove afar off counts each wandering, bottles each tear, and writes them in His book. The Dove herself is an emblem of the meek and trusting spirit, and supremely of the Lord Jesus, the harmless One among His enemies, who when He was reviled, reviled not again, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously.
webster_summary: “The silent dove of them that are afar off”; the tune over David’s psalm of trust as an exile among the Philistines.

The condition it pictures — the believer as a silent dove far from home, harmless among the hostile — is the perennial lot of the people of God in a strange land, and the temptation is to meet it with the hawk’s defences rather than the dove’s trust.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the trust of the defenceless. The dove cannot fight; she flees and mourns and waits on God, and finds that He marks her every wandering and bottles her every tear. So the exile saint, and supremely the Lord Jesus, the harmless Dove among His enemies, commits himself to Him that judgeth righteously, and is not afraid what man can do.

etymology: Rendering the Hebrew lamnattsēach, from nātsach, “to oversee, to lead, to be preeminent, to set forward”; the appointed overseer and director of the temple song.
biblical_def: “To the chief Musician” stands at the head of fifty-five psalms, and once at the close of the prophet’s song, “To the chief singer on my stringed instruments” (Hab 3:19). The word is lamnattsēach, the one set to oversee, to lead, to set the work forward; for David did not leave the praise of God to chance, but appointed chief men over the Levites “to set forward the work of the house of the LORD” (compare 1Ch 23:4), with such as Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun over the courses of song. To the chief Musician a psalm was committed, that he might teach it to the singers, set it to its proper tune, and lead the whole congregation in ordered praise. He is the picture of office and order in worship: praise rendered not as each will, but under appointed oversight, decently and in its courses. And he is a shadow of a greater Leader of praise. For Christ Himself is the true Chief Musician, who stands in the midst of the congregation to lead His brethren’s song: “I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee” (Heb 2:12). The saints do not praise alone or unled; their great Forerunner raises the tune, and the redeemed lift their voices after Him.
webster_summary: The appointed overseer and director of the temple song; a shadow of Christ, the true Leader of His people’s praise.

He is a shadow of Christ, the true Chief Musician who leads His brethren’s song.
scriptures: To the chief Musician, A Psalm for the sons of Korah.
The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds’ feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.
And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel.
Saying, I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee.
corruption_summary: An office of ordered worship; it answers the modern distaste for appointed oversight in praise, and points to Christ the true Leader of His people’s song.
corruption_paragraphs: The office of the chief Musician faces no postmodern redefinition, but the order it represents is widely resented. The age prefers a worship without appointed oversight, where each does what is right in his own eyes and spontaneity is prized above the courses David set. The chief Musician rebukes this: the praise of God was committed to appointed men, taught, tuned, and led.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is leadership and order in worship, crowned by the leadership of Christ. As the chief Musician led the temple choir, so the Lord Jesus, the true Chief Musician, stands in the midst of the church to raise the tune of praise. The saints do not sing alone or unled; their great Forerunner leads, and the redeemed lift their voices after Him.
roots_summary: Rendering the Hebrew for one set to oversee and lead, the Chief Musician directs the temple song and shadows Christ, the Leader of His people’s praise.
roots_lines: Chief Musician — Hebrew lamnattsēach, from nātsach, to oversee or lead.
The direction “to the chief Musician” heads fifty-five psalms.
To him a psalm was committed, to teach, to tune, and to lead the congregation.
Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun were set over the courses of song.
Christ is the true Chief Musician, leading praise in the midst of the church (Heb 2:12).
usage: Praise was committed to appointed men, taught, tuned, and led; not rendered as each will.
The chief Musician is the picture of office and order in the worship of God.
Christ the true Chief Musician raises the tune, and the redeemed lift their voices after Him.

etymology: Rendering the Hebrew shīr hammaialōth, “song of the goings-up” or “ascents,” from ‘ālāh, to go up; the title of fifteen psalms sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem.
biblical_def: A Song of degrees is the title borne by fifteen psalms together, the hundred-and-twentieth through the hundred-and-thirty-fourth. The Hebrew means “songs of the goings-up,” and they are most received as the pilgrim-songs of Israel, sung by the tribes as they went up to Jerusalem — the city set high upon her hills — for the three yearly feasts. Some have tied the “degrees” also to steps, whether the steps of the temple or the going-up of the soul from depth to height; for these psalms do indeed climb. They begin in distress and exile, “In my distress I cried unto the LORD” (Psa 120:1); they lift the eyes to the hills whence cometh help (Psa 121:1); they rejoice at the gates, “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD” (Psa 122:1); and they crown the ascent in the joy of brethren gathered, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psa 133:1). So the Songs of degrees map the upward way of the people of God: from the far country and the lonely tent, step by step, to the courts of the LORD and the communion of the saints. The church is ever a pilgrim church, going up; and these are her marching-songs.
webster_summary: “Songs of the goings-up”; fifteen pilgrim-psalms sung by Israel ascending to Jerusalem for the yearly feasts.
webster_full: SONG OF DEGREES, the title of fifteen psalms, the hundred-and-twentieth through hundred-and-thirty-fourth.
The Hebrew signifies “songs of the goings-up” or ascents.
They are most received as pilgrim-songs sung in going up to Jerusalem for the feasts.
Some tie the “degrees” to steps, or to the ascent of the soul from depth to height.
They climb from distress and exile to the joy of the courts of the LORD and the communion of the saints.
scriptures: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
corruption_summary: Pilgrim-psalms of the going-up; they recover the church’s upward, gathered worship against a privatized and stationary religion.
corruption_paragraphs: The Songs of degrees face no postmodern redefinition, but the corporate, ascending worship they embody is much eroded. The age makes religion a private and stationary thing — the lone soul, the solitary screen — with little sense of a people going up together to a holy place to appear before God. The pilgrim-songs rebuke that isolation; they are sung on the road, in company, climbing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church is a pilgrim people, going up together. These psalms move from the far country to the gathered courts, and they crown the ascent not in solitary rapture but in the communion of brethren dwelling in unity. The believer is glad when they say, “Let us go into the house of the LORD”; his worship is a going-up, and he does not go alone.
roots_summary: Rendering the Hebrew for “songs of the goings-up,” the Songs of degrees are fifteen pilgrim-psalms of Israel ascending to Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Song of Degrees — Hebrew shīr hammaialōth, “song of the ascents.”
Fifteen psalms bear it, the hundred-and-twentieth through hundred-and-thirty-fourth.
They are the pilgrim-songs sung in going up to Jerusalem for the feasts.
They climb from distress and exile to the joy of the LORD’s courts.
They crown the ascent in the communion of brethren dwelling in unity (Psa 133:1).
usage: The Songs of degrees map the upward way of the people of God, step by step to His courts.
The church is ever a pilgrim church, going up; these are her marching-songs.
The believer’s worship is a going-up, gathered with brethren, and he does not go alone.

etymology: Hebrew mizmōr, from zāmar, “to make music, to sing praise with instruments, to pluck the strings”; a song set to music — the very word the English “Psalm” translates.
biblical_def: Mizmor is the Hebrew word that the English “Psalm” renders, standing in the title of some fifty-seven psalms, as “A Psalm of David” (Psa 23, title) or simply “A Psalm” (Psa 98, title). It comes of a root meaning to make music, to praise with instruments, to pluck the sounding strings; and so a mizmor is not bare speech but a song framed and set to music for the worship of God. The Greek translators rendered it psalmos, whence comes our word Psalter, the book of praises. The thing itself teaches a doctrine: that God is to be praised with skill and with melody, the truth carried upon a tune, the heart lifted by the consecrated art of song. “Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms” (Psa 95:2). This is no relic of an outgrown age; the apostle binds the same threefold cord upon the church, “speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19). The mizmor abides: the people of God are a singing people, and the inspired Psalter is their first and surest songbook, the very mind of the Spirit set to music for the praise of the Most High.
webster_summary: The Hebrew word rendered “Psalm”; a song framed and set to music for the worship of God.
webster_full: MIZMOR, the Hebrew word that the English “Psalm” translates.
It comes of a root meaning to make music, to praise with instruments, to pluck the strings.
It stands in the title of some fifty-seven psalms, as “A Psalm of David.”
The Greek rendered it psalmos, whence comes our word Psalter.
It teaches that God is to be praised with skill and melody, the truth carried upon a tune.
scriptures: A Psalm. O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things.
Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms.
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.
corruption_summary: The very word “Psalm”; it recovers sung, skilful, congregational praise and the primacy of the inspired Psalter against worship reduced to mere talk or mere spectacle.
corruption_paragraphs: Mizmor faces no postmodern redefinition, but the practice it commands is pulled two ways in the present age — toward a bare and songless religion that reduces worship to talk, and toward a spectacle that prizes performance above the praise of the gathered people. The word answers both: a mizmor is a song, framed with skill, and sung to God by His people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the centrality of sung praise, and the abiding worth of the inspired Psalter. The people of God are a singing people; they are to praise Him with melody and skill, the truth borne upon a tune. The apostle keeps the mizmor in the church’s hand, bidding her sing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs; and the Book of Psalms remains her first and surest songbook, the mind of the Spirit set to music.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for making music upon the strings, Mizmor is the word rendered “Psalm” — a song set to music for the worship of God.
